plain: The Royal Navy relied on a layered air defense system during the 1982 Falklands War. Sea Harrier jump jets, launched from the carriers HMS Hermes and HMS Invincible, provided combat air patrols to intercept incoming Argentine aircraft before they could reach the task force, using their agility and AIM-9L Sidewinder missiles to notable effect. Ships like the Type 42 destroyers carried the Sea Dart missile system for medium-range air defense, while Type 22 frigates carried Sea Wolf, an effective short-range point-defense missile capable of shooting down fast, low-flying jets. Radar picket ships were positioned around the fleet to provide early warning of incoming raids. Despite these measures, several ships were still lost, including HMS Sheffield, sunk by an Exocet missile, showing the defenses were effective but not foolproof.

plain: The first ten states to ratify the U.S. Constitution and join the Union, in order, were Delaware (December 7, 1787), Pennsylvania (December 12, 1787), New Jersey (December 18, 1787), Georgia (January 2, 1788), Connecticut (January 9, 1788), Massachusetts (February 6, 1788), Maryland (April 28, 1788), South Carolina (May 23, 1788), New Hampshire (June 21, 1788), and Virginia (June 25, 1788). plain: Series I savings bonds earn interest that combines a fixed rate, set when you buy the bond and locked in for its full 30-year life, with an inflation-adjusted rate that changes every six months based on the Consumer Price Index. Unlike many other investments, this interest isn't paid out to you periodically as cash; instead, it accrues and compounds into the bond's value every month, and you only receive it when you actually redeem the bond. You must hold an I bond for at least 12 months before cashing it out, and if you redeem it before five years, you forfeit the last three months of interest as a penalty. Interest is also exempt from state and local taxes, and federal tax can be deferred until redemption.

plain: De-identification, removing or obscuring personal identifiers from data, raises several ethical concerns despite its privacy benefits. First, re-identification risk remains real: researchers have repeatedly shown that supposedly anonymized datasets can be re-identified by cross-referencing them with other available information, meaning de-identification often provides a false sense of complete safety. Second, aggressive de-identification can strip away context that matters for fairness, potentially hiding demographic patterns needed to detect bias in how systems affect different groups. Third, consent and transparency issues arise when data collected for one purpose is de-identified and repurposed for another without individuals' informed awareness. Finally, there's a power imbalance: organizations decide how de-identification is done, while the individuals whose data is used bear the actual consequences if it fails.
